checkpoints: Litmus test: ask whether a value can be computed entirely from existing props and state — if yes, it is derived, not state.

Derived values should be computed inline in render (e.g. const filtered = filterUsers(users, query)); if the computation is heavy, wrap it in useMemo, which is still derivation happening in render, not an escape into an effect.
Mirroring a derived value into a second useState synced via useEffect([query]) creates two sources of truth: query is real state, and filtered becomes a copy that must be kept aligned by hand.
Trace of one keystroke: setQuery fires first, causing render #1 where the mirrored filtered still holds the previous query's result — an out-of-phase frame the user briefly sees.
React commits that render, then the effect runs and calls setFiltered, triggering render #2 to catch the copy up — so one change costs two renders plus a moment of stale data on screen.

Initial-value hazard: because the mirror state must start somewhere (a default like []), the very first paint shows an empty list even when an empty query should show everything — a wrong value visible before the effect ever runs.

Fix: keep only non-derivable things in useState (actual user input, data from outside like a server response), treat anything computable from existing values as a plain variable recomputed every render, and reserve useEffect for genuinely synchronising with systems outside React.
An effect mirror copies the external store's value into useState only AFTER commit, so it always lags one phase behind the actual store.
Because each reader mirrors the store independently, a synchronous burst of updates can leave two readers disagreeing within the very same frame — that inconsistency is exactly what tearing is.
A mirror that subscribes only once on mount simply goes stale over time as further store updates are missed.

useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot) is React's official bridge for reading an external store without tearing, and every external state library (Zustand, Redux, Jotai's stores) sits on top of this primitive underneath.
subscribe registers so the store can tell React when it changes, and it must return a cleanup function that removes the listener.
getSnapshot reads the current value synchronously RIGHT DURING render, so every reader of the same store gets exactly one consistent snapshot per render — no tearing.
React decides to re-render only when Object.is confirms the new snapshot differs from the last one.
getServerSnapshot supplies the value used on the server and on first hydrate (where window does not yet exist).
Core critique framing: the issue is contract, not style — a child component should expose a narrow imperative API, never its raw DOM node.

Bug + fix (ref forwarding): forwardRef<HTMLInputElement> passes the <input> straight through so the parent rewrites value and style directly, breaking encapsulation and breaking the moment MessageInput restructures; fix with useImperativeHandle returning a typed handle — { focus, clear, getValue } for the input, { scrollToBottom, isAtBottom } for the list — with real DOM nodes kept in private refs so TypeScript makes any call outside that surface a compile error.

Bug + fix (ResizeObserver leak): the ResizeObserver subscription in MessageList's effect never gets released, so it outlives the component and keeps firing against a node that's already gone; the effect must return () => observer.disconnect().

Bug + fix (scroll timing): listRef.current!.scrollTop = listRef.current!.scrollHeight runs in the very same tick as setMessages, before React commits the new row, so scrollHeight is still the old value and the scroll lands one message short; defer the scroll with requestAnimationFrame (or an effect keyed on messages) so it runs after commit.
Gotcha: any useImperativeHandle deps must include whatever state the handle reads (e.g. a measured height) — an empty deps array freezes a stale value into the handle forever.
Verification (unmount test): assert the ResizeObserver never fires again after the component is gone.
Verification (e2e test): send a message and assert the list lands exactly at the bottom.
Verification (type-level check): the parent cannot call anything beyond the handle's declared surface.
Identifies that deriving visibleRows during render (not via an Effect) is the correct pattern per "You Might Not Need an Effect" — the bug is not about where the computation lives.

Explains the real problem is scope, not location: the O(n log n) filter+sort over ~20,000 rows re-runs on every render of the component, including renders that have nothing to do with rows, query or sortKey.

Identifies hoveredId as the actual trigger — it is high-frequency state (updates on every mouseover) living in the same component as the heavy derivation, so each hover causes a full re-render and thus a full re-sort.
Proposes useMemo(() => sortRows(filterRows(rows, query), sortKey), [rows, query, sortKey]) so that renders where rows/query/sortKey haven't changed reuse the cached array instead of recomputing.
Proposes moving hoveredId out of the parent component — down into each row or a small memoized child — so a hover event no longer re-renders the heavy component at all.
Explicitly flags that computing visibleRows in a useEffect + useState would NOT be a fix: the derivation still runs, and it adds an extra render pass plus a second source of truth to keep in sync.
Proposes a concrete way to verify the fix, such as profiling render duration on hover before/after, or checking that the filter/sort function is not called on renders where its inputs are unchanged.

The telemetry shows correctness is solved but the strategy is fire-and-cancel: 10 requests fired, 9 aborted — connection setup, started server work, and bandwidth wasted on requests already known to be discarded.
Layer 1 (volume): debounce the value the effect actually keys on so a request fires only once the user pauses, dropping fired count from ~10 to ~1-2 per keyword.
Layer 2 (in-flight): keep controller.abort() in cleanup — when requests do still overlap, the superseded one is truly cancelled (AbortError), not merely ignored, so the work actually stops.
Layer 3 (commit): keep the per-run ignore check — a stale response already resolved before abort() lands can still run its .then, and ignore is what stops that commit.

Senior insight: debounce changes request frequency, not the ordering guarantee — on a slow connection two debounced requests can still overlap and resolve out of order, so stripping the guards after adding debounce reintroduces the original bug.
Verify both axes: the fired/aborted counters collapse after debouncing, and the deterministic slow-then-fast race test still commits the newest keyword with the guards in place.
Split the API into two lanes: props are the declarative lane (messages array plus presentation config) — React owns "what is shown", and every screen passes its own data.

The imperative lane is a MessageListHandle type exposing exactly scrollToBottom(), isAtBottom(), and getMeasuredHeight() — operations that only exist in the DOM after layout and are one-shot actions, not renderable state.
Mechanically, forwardRef<MessageListHandle, MessageListProps> wraps the component to receive a ref, while the real scroll container stays in a private scrollRef the parent never sees.
useImperativeHandle(ref, factory, deps) builds the returned handle object from that private scrollRef — this is the mechanism that turns the private ref into the public contract.
The handle type IS the public contract — a parent typing its ref as useRef<MessageListHandle> gets a compile-time error the instant it reaches for anything not on the list.

getMeasuredHeight() reads a measuredHeight state kept in sync by a ResizeObserver (disconnected in effect cleanup), so the useImperativeHandle deps array must include measuredHeight or the handle closes over the mount-time height and callers get a stale number forever.

The raw container is never exposed, on purpose: handing out the node gives callers direct DOM power and locks the component's internals in place, so any future change would silently break every caller.
A narrow, typed handle is what lets one component serve three screens today and still change shape tomorrow.
createExternalStore<T>(initial) returns exactly the three pieces useSyncExternalStore needs: subscribe, getSnapshot, and setSnapshot.

subscribe(listener) adds the listener to an internal Set<Listener> and must return a cleanup () => listeners.delete(listener) — the function React calls on unmount or when subscribe changes reference, and forgetting it leaks the listener.
getSnapshot() reads the current value synchronously during render, not after commit like useEffect, which is exactly why there is no phase gap that causes tearing.

getSnapshot must return the same reference while the data is unchanged (React compares via Object.is) — a fresh object literal every call triggers infinite re-renders with a "getSnapshot should be cached" warning, so composite snapshots must cache the reference and only build a new one when the value truly changes.
setSnapshot(next) guards with if (Object.is(value, next)) return before writing and notifying, so change-detection lives in exactly one place rather than scattered across readers.

The store should be a module-scope singleton with subscribe/getSnapshot kept as stable references that are never redefined per render, so multiple components read it without a Provider or Context wrapper, and useSyncExternalStore guarantees every reader gets one consistent snapshot within the same frame, even through a burst of setSnapshot calls.

For the async case, the "commit only if still the latest result" logic must live inside the store via an increasing id assigned per operation, writing the result only if its id is still latest — keeping this in the store gives a single arbiter, unlike each component tracking its own last-request-id.
SSR requires a third getServerSnapshot parameter returning a safe, browser-independent default, since the server has no window — otherwise the first hydrate throws or mismatches.

Submitting is a user action, so the send-request-and-show-confirmation logic belongs directly in the onSubmit handler, where you know exactly which action occurred and can run it once at the right moment.
Routing it through a submitted flag plus useEffect instead models a one-shot action as state.
The Effect loses the action context — it only sees that submitted just changed, not whether this is a real submit or some other code path that flipped the flag.
It runs on React's schedule rather than the user's, so the send is decoupled from the actual submit moment.
It must reset the flag itself, adding an extra render cycle that is prone to loops.
In dev, StrictMode double-invoking Effects can duplicate the send.

The classifying question is: does this happen because the user just did something (event handler), or because the component is showing and must sync with something outside React (Effect) — here it is unambiguously the former.
Effects should be reserved for genuine synchronization with systems outside React, such as a subscription or syncing data over the network tied to the component being on screen.
Identifies `messages` as the only genuine declarative state in this problem, since React must re-render the list whenever it changes.
States that focus, clear, and scroll are one-shot DOM imperatives with no corresponding displayed state, so they should not be modeled as state at all.
Explains the core flaw in the colleague's `shouldFocus` proposal: it forces a one-shot action into data, requiring an extra `useEffect` to read that state and manually reset it back to `false`.
Gives the concrete failure case for `shouldFocus`: sending two messages back to back can let the first effect's reset race the second `set` call, causing a missed or dropped focus.
Proposes refs as the right mechanism: the parent (`ChatComposer`) holds a typed ref to each child (`MessageInput`, `MessageList`) instead of routing the action through shared state.
Names `forwardRef` + `useImperativeHandle` as how each child exposes a narrow imperative API (e.g. `focus`/`clear` on the input, `scrollToBottom` on the list) while keeping its real DOM node private.

Identifies the scroll timing subtlety: `setMessages` only schedules a render, so the new row isn't in the DOM yet when scrolling runs immediately after — the fix is to wait for commit, e.g. via `requestAnimationFrame`.
Bonus: notes that an uncontrolled input keeps its text in the DOM rather than React state, so `clear()` can just reset the DOM value directly without ever causing the parent to re-render.
Both `useState` and `useRef` survive across renders, but only a state setter talks to React's render scheduler — assigning `ref.current` is silent and React neither watches it nor reacts to it.

That difference is the whole decision rule: a ref is for anything that must persist across renders but is never meant to drive what's on screen — a DOM node, a timer id, an imperative handle; equivalently, if the UI must reflect the value it's state's job, if you only need it to persist across renders and read it imperatively it's a ref's job.

Get the direction wrong one way and store UI-facing data in a ref: the value changes but the screen doesn't, because nothing ever asked React to re-render — the UI silently drifts out of sync with the real value.

Get it wrong the other way and track a render-independent value, like a render counter or timer id, in state: every write is also a state update, which re-renders the component, which runs the write again — a self-amplifying loop that can spin forever.

The same counter kept in a ref instead increments quietly with no re-render at all, the same category as the lesson's timer-id example — confirming a ref, not state, is where render-independent bookkeeping belongs.
